title: -ar verbs
topic: present tense of regular -ar verbs; negation with no
why: After ser and tener, here's the first big conjugation pattern: regular -ar verbs, by far the most common. With the negation no, you can already talk about your job, your studies and what you don't do.

Hablar, trabajar, estudiar: the present of -ar verbs

The great majority of Spanish verbs end in -ar. They're all conjugated the same way: remove -ar and add an ending that tells you who's doing the action.

hablar (to speak)trabajar (to work)estudiar (to study)
yohablotrabajoestudio
túhablastrabajasestudias
él, ella, ustedhablatrabajaestudia
nosotros, nosotrashablamostrabajamosestudiamos
vosotros, vosotrashabláistrabajáisestudiáis
ellos, ellas, ustedeshablantrabajanestudian

In English the verb barely changes (\"I speak, you speak, we speak, they speak\": only \"he speaks\" gets an -s), so you need the pronoun. In Spanish every ending is different and clearly heard: hablo, hablas, habla, hablan. That's why the subject is usually dropped.

Hablo francés y estudio español.I speak French and I'm studying Spanish.

Traps for an English speaker

  • Each person has its own ending: with yo it's -o, so \"I speak\" is hablo. Don't reuse a single form for everyone, as English does with \"speak\".
  • With vosotros, the written accent is required: habláis, trabajáis.
  • With usted (polite \"you\"), use the él form: ¿Usted habla francés? (Do you speak French?)
  • As in English, languages take no article after hablar and estudiar, but they're lowercase: Hablo inglés, Estudio español.

Tip: the nosotros ending is -amos, the ellos ending is -an. Think \"me and my friends\" → hablamos: an m for \"we\", an n for \"they\".

", "

Today's verbs

All these verbs are regular: they follow the hablar pattern exactly. Knowing the infinitive is enough to conjugate them.

VerbMeaningExample
escucharto listen (to)Escucho la radio.
mirarto look at, to watchMiras el móvil.
comprarto buyCompra un libro.
tomarto have (a drink, food)Tomamos un café.
llegarto arriveLlegáis tarde.
buscarto look forBuscan trabajo.
necesitarto needNecesito un ordenador.
desayunarto have breakfastDesayuno en casa.
cenarto have dinnerCenamos tarde.

Notice two things:

  • desayunar and cenar are verbs: one word for \"to have breakfast\" and \"to have dinner\".
  • necesitar works just like \"to need\", with no extra word: Necesito un café (I need a coffee). It can also be followed by an infinitive: Necesito trabajar.

Me llamo: a set phrase

To give your name, Spanish doesn't say \"my name is\" but \"I call myself\". It's a reflexive verb, which we'll study later. For now, learn these forms as set phrases:

SpanishEnglish
me llamomy name is
te llamasyour name is
se llamahis, her name is; your name is (usted)
—¿Cómo te llamas? —Me llamo Lucía.—What's your name? —My name is Lucía.

To take the bus, in Spain you say coger el autobús. Tomar is mainly for what you drink or eat, like \"to have\" in English: tomar un café, tomar una cerveza.

", "

Negation: no

English needs a helper to say no: \"I don't work\", \"she doesn't speak\". Spanish has no \"do\" at all: just put no right before the verb.

No trabajo los sábados.I don't work on Saturdays.
Marta no habla alemán.Marta doesn't speak German.
No me llamo Ana, me llamo Elena.My name isn't Ana, it's Elena.

When answering a question with \"no\", you'll often hear two no: the first one answers the question, the second one negates the verb.

—¿Hablas inglés? —No, no hablo inglés.—Do you speak English? —No, I don't speak English.

Questions

As with ser and tener, a yes/no question is made with intonation only: no \"do\", the sentence doesn't change, only your voice rises at the end.

SpanishEnglish
Trabajas en Madrid.You work in Madrid.
¿Trabajas en Madrid?Do you work in Madrid?
No trabajas en Madrid.You don't work in Madrid.
¿No trabajas en Madrid?Don't you work in Madrid?

To say \"on Saturdays\" (every Saturday), Spanish uses the article: los sábados. The days of the week will come later; for now, just remember this phrase.

Don't look for a Spanish \"do\" or \"don't\": \"I don't work\" is simply no trabajo, never \"trabajo no\".
